question: What does the acronym BRRETA stand for, and where is it codified in the Official Code of Georgia?
choice_a: The Broker Regulation and Real Estate Transaction Act, codified at O.C.G.A. Title 43, Chapter 40
choice_b: The Buyer Representation and Real Estate Trust Act, codified at O.C.G.A. Title 44, Chapter 5
choice_c: The Brokerage Relationships in Real Estate Transactions Act, codified at O.C.G.A. Title 10, Chapter 6A
choice_d: The Brokerage Records and Real Estate Transfer Act, codified at O.C.G.A. Title 48, Chapter 6
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-1 states that the chapter 'shall be known and may be cited as the Brokerage Relationships in Real Estate Transactions Act,' and BRRETA is codified in Title 10, Chapter 6A -- not in the general license-law chapter, Title 43-40.

question: By default, and absent an express written agreement to the contrary, what standard of duty does BRRETA impose on a Georgia real estate broker toward the broker's own client?
choice_a: A full common-law fiduciary duty, identical to that owed by a trustee to a trust beneficiary
choice_b: No duty of any kind unless a separate written contract is signed
choice_c: A strict-liability duty under which the broker guarantees the outcome of the transaction
choice_d: A statutory duty of reasonable care in discharging the broker's specified statutory duties, rather than an automatic common-law fiduciary duty
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-4(a) displaces the common-law fiduciary standard by default: a broker 'shall not be deemed to have a fiduciary relationship with any party or fiduciary obligations to any party but shall only be responsible for exercising reasonable care' in discharging the statutory duties, unless the parties expressly agree otherwise in writing.

question: BRRETA sets out separate statutory duty provisions depending on which party a broker is engaged to represent. Which of the following correctly identifies that structure?
choice_a: Sections 10-6A-5 through 10-6A-8 set out distinct statutory duties for a broker engaged by a seller, a landlord, a buyer, and a tenant, respectively
choice_b: BRRETA sets out only a single, undifferentiated duty section that applies identically no matter which party the broker represents
choice_c: BRRETA's duty sections apply only to brokers representing buyers; seller representation is governed entirely by common law
choice_d: BRRETA's duty sections apply only to residential transactions and have no provisions for landlords or tenants
explanation: O.C.G.A. Sections 10-6A-5 through 10-6A-8 lay out separate statutory duty provisions for single-agency relationships: broker engaged by a seller, by a landlord, by a buyer, and by a tenant, respectively.

question: Does BRRETA permit a Georgia broker to act as a dual agent, representing both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction?
choice_a: No, dual agency is categorically prohibited under Georgia law in all circumstances
choice_b: Yes, dual agency is expressly permitted under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-12, provided all clients give written consent meeting specified content requirements
choice_c: Yes, but only with the verbal consent of just one of the two clients
choice_d: Dual agency is permitted only if the transaction involves commercial property, never residential property
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-12 expressly permits dual agency where all clients give written consent that meets the statute's specified content requirements; dual agency is not banned outright in Georgia.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-12, what must the written consent for dual agency include regarding the description of the arrangement?
choice_a: A guarantee that the dual agent will obtain the highest possible price for the seller and the lowest possible price for the buyer simultaneously
choice_b: A waiver of the client's right to be represented by any other broker in the future
choice_c: A description of the transaction types in which the broker will act as a dual agent
choice_d: A notarized statement from the Georgia Real Estate Commission approving the specific transaction
explanation: Section 10-6A-12 requires the dual-agency written consent to include, among other things, a description of the transaction types in which the broker will act as a dual agent for the parties.

question: Besides describing the transaction types involved, what else must a valid dual-agency written consent under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-12 state about the parties' interests?
choice_a: A statement that the buyer's and seller's interests are always perfectly aligned in a dual-agency transaction
choice_b: A statement waiving each client's right to receive any disclosures at all during the transaction
choice_c: A statement that the dual agent will act exclusively on behalf of whichever client pays a higher commission
choice_d: A statement that the dual agent represents two clients whose interests may be potentially adverse to one another
explanation: Section 10-6A-12 requires the written consent to include a statement that the dual agent represents two clients whose interests may be potentially adverse, so both clients understand the nature of the divided representation before consenting.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-12's dual-agency consent requirements, what must the consent disclose about material facts and confidential information?
choice_a: A statement that the dual agent will disclose material facts to all parties, except confidential information a client has restricted
choice_b: A statement that the dual agent will keep all information, including material facts affecting the property, completely confidential from both parties
choice_c: A statement that only the seller's confidential financial information will ever be disclosed to the buyer
choice_d: A statement that material fact disclosure is entirely optional and left to the dual agent's sole discretion
explanation: Section 10-6A-12 requires the written consent to state that the dual agent will disclose material facts to all parties except for confidential information a client has specifically restricted from disclosure, balancing transparency with client-directed confidentiality.

question: What is 'designated agency' as recognized under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-13?
choice_a: An arrangement in which a single licensee is designated by the Georgia Real Estate Commission to handle every transaction in a given county
choice_b: An arrangement in which different affiliated licensees of the same firm are assigned as exclusive designated agents to different clients in the same transaction, each owing full statutory duties only to their own client
choice_c: A form of subagency in which a cooperating broker automatically represents the listing broker's client without any separate agreement
choice_d: An arrangement that requires the buyer and seller to be represented by licensees from two entirely unrelated brokerage firms
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-13 expressly recognizes designated agency: a broker may assign different affiliated licensees as designated agents to represent different clients exclusively in the same transaction, with each designated agent owing the full statutory duties under Sections 10-6A-5 through 10-6A-8 to their own client only.

question: In a designated agency arrangement under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-13, to whom does each designated agent owe the full statutory duties set out in Sections 10-6A-5 through 10-6A-8?
choice_a: Equally to both the buyer and the seller in the transaction, regardless of which one the licensee was assigned to represent
choice_b: Only to the qualifying broker of the firm, not to either the buyer or the seller
choice_c: Only to the designated agent's own client, not to the other party's designated agent's client
choice_d: To whichever party's interests the licensee personally believes are more deserving of protection
explanation: Under Section 10-6A-13, each designated agent owes the full statutory duties only to the client that agent was specifically assigned to represent, allowing different affiliated licensees within the same firm to represent opposing clients in the same deal without each owing duties to the other's client.

question: Which of the following brokerage relationship structures are affirmatively recognized within BRRETA's statutory framework?
choice_a: Only single agency; BRRETA makes no provision at all for either dual or designated agency
choice_b: Only dual agency; BRRETA prohibits single-party representation entirely
choice_c: Only designated agency; single agency and dual agency were both repealed when BRRETA was enacted
choice_d: Single agency (to a seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant), dual agency with proper written consent, and designated agency
explanation: BRRETA's structure affirmatively recognizes single agency to a seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant under Sections 10-6A-5 through 10-6A-8, dual agency with proper written consent under Section 10-6A-12, and designated agency under Section 10-6A-13.

question: A broker's firm has an accepted offer where the buyer and seller are each represented by a different affiliated licensee of the same firm, with written consent obtained meeting BRRETA's dual-agency content requirements. What is this arrangement most accurately described as under BRRETA?
choice_a: Designated agency, since two different licensees within the firm are each assigned to represent one client exclusively
choice_b: An unauthorized arrangement, since BRRETA requires the same individual licensee to represent both parties personally
choice_c: A per se unfair trade practice regardless of consent obtained
choice_d: Subagency, since both licensees ultimately answer to the same qualifying broker
explanation: When different affiliated licensees of the same firm are each assigned to represent a different client in the same transaction, with each owing full statutory duties only to their own client, that arrangement is designated agency under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-13.

question: A Georgia broker represents a seller under a single-agency relationship and has not entered into any separate written agreement expanding the broker's duties. Under BRRETA, is the broker automatically bound by common-law fiduciary duties such as undivided loyalty and full disclosure of all information?
choice_a: Yes -- every single-agency relationship in Georgia automatically carries full common-law fiduciary obligations
choice_b: No -- absent an express written agreement to the contrary, the broker owes the statutory duty of reasonable care under BRRETA rather than an automatic common-law fiduciary duty
choice_c: Yes, but only if the seller is an individual rather than a business entity
choice_d: No -- single agents in Georgia owe no duties whatsoever to their own clients
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-4(a) displaces the common-law fiduciary standard by default for all brokerage relationships, including single agency, replacing it with a statutory duty of reasonable care unless the parties expressly agree in writing to a fiduciary relationship.

question: Under general agency-law principles applicable to real estate practice, what is the fundamental difference between a 'client' and a 'customer' in a brokered transaction?
choice_a: There is no legal distinction between the two terms; they describe the same relationship
choice_b: A customer always pays the broker's commission, while a client never does
choice_c: A client is a party the broker represents in an agency relationship owing specified duties, while a customer is a party the broker assists in a transaction without representing that party as an agent
choice_d: A client is any party who has signed a listing agreement, while a customer is any party who has closed on a property in the past
explanation: As a matter of general real estate agency principles reflected in brokerage-relationship statutes like BRRETA, a client is represented by the broker under an agency relationship carrying specified duties, while a customer is a party the broker deals with or assists in the transaction without an agency relationship.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate agency-law terminology, consistent with BRRETA's client/customer distinction but not a specific Georgia statutory citation in this question

question: In general real estate practice, why is it important for a licensee to clarify early in a transaction whether a prospective party is being represented as a client or merely assisted as a customer?
choice_a: Because Georgia law requires this clarification only for commercial transactions, never for residential ones
choice_b: Because the distinction only affects who signs the closing documents, not the duties owed
choice_c: Because customers are legally prohibited from ever becoming clients later in the same transaction
choice_d: Because the scope of duties owed, including the level of advocacy and confidentiality, differs significantly between an agency relationship and a non-agency working relationship
explanation: Clarifying the nature of the relationship matters because an agency relationship carries a different, generally more protective scope of duties (advocacy, confidentiality, and disclosure obligations) than a non-agency, ministerial-assistance relationship with a customer.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate agency-law principle

question: Under general agency principles applicable to real estate brokerage, what does the duty of 'obedience' typically require of an agent representing a client?
choice_a: Following the client's lawful instructions within the scope of the agency relationship
choice_b: Following any instruction from the client, even one that would require violating the law
choice_c: Ignoring the client's instructions whenever the agent believes a different course of action would be more profitable
choice_d: Obeying instructions only from the client's attorney, never from the client directly
explanation: Under general agency-law doctrine, the duty of obedience requires an agent to follow the client's lawful instructions within the scope of the representation; an agent is not obligated (and generally not permitted) to follow an instruction requiring an illegal act.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate agency-law doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific

question: Under general agency principles applicable to real estate brokerage, what does the duty of 'accounting' typically require of a licensee handling a client's funds or documents?
choice_a: Investing the client's earnest money in the licensee's personal business ventures for the client's benefit
choice_b: Properly safeguarding, tracking, and providing a true accounting of any funds, property, or documents entrusted to the licensee in the course of the agency
choice_c: Withholding all financial records from the client until the transaction has fully closed
choice_d: Providing an accounting only if the client is a corporation rather than an individual
explanation: The general agency-law duty of accounting requires a licensee to properly handle, track, and be able to account for any money, property, or documents entrusted to them in the course of representing a client, distinct from and consistent with Georgia's separate statutory trust-account requirements.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate agency-law doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific

question: A buyer asks their designated agent, under a BRRETA-compliant designated agency arrangement, to disclose confidential settlement-flexibility information that the buyer specifically told the agent to keep confidential. Consistent with BRRETA's statutory duty framework, what should the designated agent do?
choice_a: Immediately disclose the confidential information to the seller's designated agent regardless of the buyer's instruction
choice_b: Disclose the information only if the seller offers to pay a higher commission
choice_c: Withhold that confidential information, since the agent's statutory duty runs only to the buyer and material-fact disclosure obligations to the other party do not override a client's specific confidentiality restriction
choice_d: Refuse to represent the buyer further unless the buyer waives all confidentiality
explanation: Consistent with BRRETA's designated-agency structure, a designated agent owes full statutory duties only to their own client, and the dual-agency disclosure framework under Section 10-6A-12 itself recognizes that a client may restrict certain confidential information from disclosure -- so a designated agent should honor a client's specific confidentiality instruction.
source_note: O.C.G.A. Sections 10-6A-12, 10-6A-13 (applied to a designated-agency scenario)
